title: Urine output per kg per hour and hourly totals
blurb: Work out average hourly urine output and mL/kg/hour for adults, children and babies, and compare it with a threshold given in the stem.
question: A woman weighing 64 kg passes 128 mL of urine over 4 hours. What is her urine output in mL/kg/hour?

teach.h: Urine output per kg per hour
teach.body: Formal rule: urine output (mL/kg/hour) = total urine (mL) ÷ weight (kg) ÷ number of hours. Average hourly output (mL/hour) = total urine ÷ hours. Plain English: share the urine out over the hours, then over each kilogram. It lets you compare a small baby and a large adult on the same scale.

steps.label: Compare
steps.sub: With the threshold in the stem

teach.h: Worked example: Tom on a high-dependency unit
teach.body: Tom Walsh weighs 80 kg and has a catheter after surgery. Hourly volumes: 45, 38, 30 and 27 mL. Total = 140 mL over 4 hours. Average = 140 ÷ 4 = 35 mL/hour. Per kg = 35 ÷ 80 = 0.4375, so 0.44 mL/kg/hour to two decimal places. Sense-check: 35 mL from an 80 kg man is well under 1 mL per kg each hour.

Escalation thresholds are set by guidance and local policy, so a Part A stem will state the figure it wants you to use, for example "the escalation threshold is 0.5 mL/kg/hour". To find the smallest hourly volume that meets it, multiply: threshold × weight. For a 70 kg woman and 0.5 mL/kg/hour that is 35 mL each hour. Use the stem's number, not one from memory.

teach.text: Dividing by only one of the two: 140 ÷ 80 = 1.75 is mL per kg over the whole 4 hours, not per hour, and makes a low output look four times better. Divide by the weight AND the hours.

teach.body: Babies' weights are often in grams: convert to kg first (3200 g = 3.2 kg). Wet nappies are weighed; the stem will say 1 g = 1 mL, so 22 g of urine is 22 mL. Then use the same formula: total mL ÷ kg ÷ hours.

items: Convert grams to kg before dividing.
Classic error: dividing by weight or hours, not both.
Thresholds: use the figure printed in the stem.

summary: You can now total hourly urine volumes and convert them to mL/hour and mL/kg/hour, including babies weighed in grams. You can also turn a threshold given in the stem into the smallest acceptable hourly volume.

A.q: A man weighing 70 kg passes 210 mL of urine over 6 hours. What is his average urine output? Write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Divided by weight only: this is mL/kg over 6 hours.
whyNot.1: Divided by hours only: this is mL/hour.

A.q: A woman's hourly catheter urine volumes over 5 hours are 42, 36, 28, 30 and 24 mL. What is her average hourly urine output?
A.why: Total = 160 mL. Average = 160 ÷ 5 = 32 mL per hour.

whyNot.1: This is the 5-hour total, not the hourly average.
whyNot.2: Divided by 4; there are 5 hourly volumes.
whyNot.3: Took the last hour instead of the average.

A.q: A child weighing 15 kg passes 180 mL of urine over 8 hours. What is the average urine output? Write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.3: Divided the weight by the hours; the urine volume is missing.

B.q: A woman weighs 75 kg. Her unit's escalation threshold for urine output is 0.5 mL/kg/hour. What is the smallest hourly urine volume that meets this threshold? Write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Divided the weight by the threshold instead of multiplying.
whyNot.1: Used 0.05 instead of 0.5 mL/kg/hour: 0.05 × 75 = 3.75, which rounds to 3.8.
whyNot.2: Gave the volume for 3 hours (37.5 × 3); the question asks for one hour.

B.q: A man weighing 90 kg has hourly catheter urine volumes of 30 mL, 25 mL and 20 mL. What is his average urine output over the 3 hours? Write your answer to two decimal places.
B.why: Total 75 mL ÷ 3 hours = 25 mL/hour. 25 ÷ 90 = 0.2777..., so 0.28 mL/kg/hour.

whyNot.0: Divided by weight only (mL/kg over 3 hours).

B.q: A baby weighing 3.2 kg has four wet nappies over 12 hours containing 18 g, 24 g, 20 g and 26 g of urine (1 g = 1 mL). What is the average urine output? Write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.3: Rounded to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

C.q: A man weighing 82 kg has hourly catheter urine volumes of 40, 35, 30, 25, 20 and 15 mL over 6 hours. What is his average urine output? Write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.1: Divided by hours only; that is mL/hour.

C.q: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia weighs 68 kg. Her unit's escalation threshold for urine output is 0.5 mL/kg/hour. What is the smallest total urine volume over 4 hours that meets this threshold?
C.why: Per hour = 0.5 × 68 = 34 mL. Over 4 hours = 34 × 4 = 136 mL.

whyNot.1: This is the volume for one hour, not four.
whyNot.2: Divided by the threshold instead of multiplying.

C.q: A child weighing 22 kg is on a 24-hour fluid balance chart. Urine: 0600 120 mL, 1200 150 mL, 1800 130 mL, 2400 140 mL. What is the average urine output over the 24 hours? Write your answer to two decimal places.

reteach.title: Divide twice: hours, then kilograms
reteach.question: A 60 kg woman passes 120 mL in 4 hours. What is her output in mL/kg/hour?

blocks.body: 120 ÷ 4 = 30 mL each hour. 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 mL/kg/hour. Either order works, as long as both divisions happen.

blocks.text: Stopping after one division (30, or 2) gives a number that looks far too high or describes the wrong unit.

test.q: A woman weighing 60 kg passes 120 mL of urine over 4 hours. What is her average urine output?

whyNot.3: Multiplied by the hours instead of dividing.

explain.body: Average mL/hour = total ÷ number of hours.

test.q: A man passes 150 mL of urine in total over 6 hours. What is his average hourly urine output?

whyNot.0: This is the total, not the hourly average.

explain.body: Divide a baby's weight in grams by 1000 before using it: 3500 g = 3.5 kg.

test.q: A baby weighing 3500 g passes 42 mL of urine over 6 hours. What is the average urine output?
A man weighs 58 kg. The ward's escalation threshold for urine output is 0.5 mL/kg/hour. What is the smallest hourly urine volume that meets it?

whyNot.1: Divided the weight by the threshold.
